title: Franchise Financing Underwriting: How Lenders Evaluate Units and Brands
summary: Franchise financing underwriting scores two kinds of risk: the unit (cash flow, equity, guarantees, and collateral) and the brand (FDD Items 7, 19, 20, and 21). This guide covers SBA SOP 50 10 8.1 minimums, acquisition rules, the Franchise Directory, and a step-by-step underwriting framework.
body_markdown:
Franchise financing underwriting is how lenders decide whether a franchisee can repay a loan by analyzing the individual unit and the brand behind it together. Lenders test the unit through cash flow coverage, equity injection, guarantees, and collateral. They test the brand through the Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD), especially Items 7, 19, 20, and 21.


For SBA 7(a) loans, the rules come from[SBA SOP 50 10 8.1](https://www.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs) , which applies to applications on or after October 1, 2026. Conventional lenders and fintechs are not bound by the SOP, but credit teams can use its thresholds as a reference standard for franchise loans.


This guide covers required documents, current DSCR and equity minimums, guaranty and collateral rules, and acquisition rules for existing locations. It also explains the reinstated SBA Franchise Directory and offers a step-by-step framework your risk team can apply to any franchise credit.


‍


### Franchise Financing Underwriting Evaluates the Unit and the Brand


A franchise loan carries the risk of a single small business plus the risk of the system it operates inside. Strong underwriting separates those two layers, scores each one, and then decides how much one can offset the other.


#### Unit-Level Risk Comes Down to Cash Flow and the Operator


At the unit level, lenders ask whether this location, run by this operator, will generate enough cash to service all of its debt. The core inputs are projected or historical cash flow, the owner's equity contribution, personal guarantees, available collateral, and the operator's management experience.


For a new unit with no operating history, cash flow evidence is projected rather than historical. That makes the quality of the projection, and the franchisor data behind it, central to the credit decision.


#### Brand-Level Risk Lives in the FDD


At the brand level, lenders ask whether the franchise system gives units a reasonable chance of success and whether the franchisor is financially stable. The FTC Franchise Rule at[16 CFR 436.5](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-436/subpart-C/section-436.5) requires four disclosures that matter most to credit teams:


- **Item 7 (Estimated Initial Investment):** A franchisor-estimated table of startup costs, including an "Additional funds" line for at least the first three months or a reasonable period for the industry.
- **Item 19 (Financial Performance Representations):** Optional. If included, it must have written substantiation and disclose how many outlets attained the stated results.
- **Item 20 (Outlet Data):** Three fiscal years of openings, terminations, non-renewals, reacquisitions, and other closures, plus contact lists for current and former franchisees.
- **Item 21 (Financial Statements):** Franchisor financials audited by an independent CPA, with a phase-in that allows unaudited statements for start-up franchisors.


Because Item 19 is optional, lenders cannot assume performance data exists. When it does, underwriters should check its scope, because a figure drawn from a subset of outlets does not represent a system average.


#### Brand Risk Varies Widely Across Systems


Vendor data suggests historical loss outcomes differ widely between brand risk tiers. An[October 2025 FRANdata analysis](https://frandata.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Correlation-between-FRANdata-FUND-Scores.pdf) covered more than 18,000 SBA 7(a) franchise loans. Brands in its "High Risk" tier showed roughly a 15% historical charge-off rate, compared with under 2% for its "Minimal Risk" tier.


Treat these figures carefully, because they are vendor-produced, historical charge-off results for FRANdata's own scoring product rather than default forecasts for new loans. The middle tiers were also not strictly ordered (5.3% for "Average" versus 5.6% for "Low"), and FRANdata described the overall brand-level relationship as modest.

### SBA 7(a) Thresholds Give Every Lender a Reference Standard


SOP 50 10 8.1 sets coverage, equity, and guaranty floors that vary by loan type. The figures below reflect the SOP as of October 1, 2026. Some content still describes the older SOP 50 10 8, so confirm which version a source uses before relying on it.


#### DSCR Minimums by Loan Scenario


Coverage is the primary test because the SOP treats the applicant's cash flow as the primary source of repayment, ahead of any collateral recovery. Debt service includes principal and interest on all business debt, including the new loan.


Loan scenario (SOP 50 10 8.1) Minimum DSCR Cash flow basis Key condition


Standard 7(a), including new franchise units 1.15:1 (1:1 global) Historical and/or projected Start-ups must project 1.15 within 2 years of funding


7(a) Small, $350,000 or less, not a change of ownership 1.10:1 Historical or projected Projections use a 1-year window


Change of ownership: initial acquisition 1.25:1 Last fiscal year-end or two-year average New in 8.1; earlier versions used 1.15


Change of ownership: owner buyout 1.25:1 Last fiscal year-end or two-year average Equity may be reduced with sufficient liquidity


Change of ownership: business expansion 1.15:1 Last fiscal year-end or two-year average Equity may be reduced with sufficient liquidity


#### Equity Injection Requirements


SBA considers an equity injection of at least 10% of total project costs necessary for a start-up, meaning a business operating one year or less. A new franchise unit with no operating history falls into this category, and project costs exclude lines of credit and 504 loans.


Acceptable sources include unborrowed cash, a personal loan repayable from a non-business source, and full-standby debt. Business credit cards are not on the list, and lenders must verify the injection before disbursement.


#### Personal Guaranty and Collateral Rules


Any individual with direct or indirect ownership of 20% or more must provide an unlimited full guaranty. Lenders may also require additional guarantors when credit reasons warrant it. A loan must not be declined solely because collateral is inadequate, yet the SBA guaranty is no substitute for available collateral.


The "fully secured" test values available fixed assets at set haircuts:


- New equipment is valued at 75% of purchase price.
- Used equipment is valued at 50% of net book value, or 80% with an orderly liquidation value appraisal.
- Improved real estate is valued at 85%.
- Personal real estate is not required when the borrower's equity in it is under 25%.


‍


### Buying an Existing Franchise Location Requires Stricter Coverage


Acquisitions of existing units, often called franchise resales, fall under the change-of-ownership rules in Appendix 15 of SOP 50 10 8.1. These rules are tighter than start-up rules in two important ways.


First, an initial acquisition requires a 1.25:1 DSCR measured on the last fiscal year-end or a two-year average.


Second, the 10% equity injection for an initial acquisition cannot be reduced or eliminated. Appendix 15 also places limits on seller standby debt and similar equity sources. Credit teams should confirm the current terms in the[SOP](https://www.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs) before structuring a seller note.


For non-SBA lenders, these rules offer a useful benchmark. An existing unit has a track record, so its historical financials usually give firmer evidence than a franchisor's projections for a new site.


‍


### What Changed in SBA Franchise Eligibility


SBA reinstated the Franchise Directory with[SOP 50 10 8](https://www.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs) , effective June 1, 2025. Under SOP 50 10 8.1, any brand that meets the FTC definition of a franchise must appear on the Directory to obtain SBA financing.


According to[SBA's Franchise Directory page](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/plan-your-business/buy-existing-business-or-franchise/sba-franchise-directory) , lenders can now rely on the Directory and no longer need to review franchise documents for affiliation or eligibility. The Directory is published as an Excel file on SBA.gov and updated weekly.


The process and its limits are worth understanding:


- Under[SOP 50 10 8.1](https://www.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs) , lenders must check the Directory before submitting a non-delegated loan or approving a delegated loan.
- If the brand is not listed, the lender cannot submit or approve the SBA loan, per[SOP 50 10 8.1](https://www.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs) .
- Franchisors apply by sending the franchise agreement, FDD, and other documents to franchise@sba.gov.
- Franchisors must then execute SBA's Franchisor Certification to be listed.
- Listing confirms SBA eligibility under the franchise relationship, and[SOP 50 10 8.1](https://www.sba.gov/document/sop-50-10-lender-development-company-loan-programs) states it is not an endorsement or guaranty of brand success.


That last point matters for credit teams. Directory status answers an eligibility question, so brand quality still has to be assessed through the FDD and franchisor data.


‍


### A Step-by-Step Franchise Loan Underwriting Framework


The following framework combines SBA requirements with brand-level analysis. Non-SBA lenders can adopt the same sequence and adjust thresholds to their own credit policy.


1. **Confirm eligibility first.** For SBA loans, check the brand against the current Franchise Directory. Review any management agreements outside the listed FDD for passive-business ineligibility.
2. **Collect the core document set.** Request the FDD, franchise agreement, borrower projections, franchisor-provided cash flow projections, equity source records, guarantor information, and a collateral schedule.
3. **Size the full project cost.** Use FDD Item 7 to confirm the request covers build-out, opening costs, and the additional funds period.
4. **Analyze brand performance.** Use Item 20 to track three years of terminations, non-renewals, reacquisitions, and closures, and review Item 21 for franchisor financial strength.
5. **Review failed-franchisee data.** The SOP requires lenders to review credit information the franchisor provides, such as the number of failed franchisees and cash flow projections.
6. **Stress the unit's cash flow.** Test projections against the applicable DSCR floor, and check whether Item 19 data comes from all outlets or a subset.
7. **Verify equity and guarantees.** Confirm the injection meets the 10% minimum from eligible sources, and collect unlimited guarantees from every owner holding 20% or more.
8. **Assess collateral.** Apply the fully secured haircuts, and document the reasoning when a cash-flow-strong loan is approved with a collateral shortfall.
9. **Document the decision.** Record which SOP version, DSCR basis, and brand data informed the approval, so reviewers can trace each condition.


For acquisitions, add the seller's last fiscal year-end or two-year historical financials to step 2. Then apply the 1.25:1 coverage test in step 6.


‍


### Franchise Financing Underwriting Best Practices That Keep Decisions Consistent


Franchise credit goes wrong when teams treat brand signals as proof of unit quality or apply one threshold to every loan type. These practices help credit teams avoid both mistakes.


#### Recommendations for Franchise Credit Teams


- **Date-stamp every SBA rule.** Cite SOP 50 10 8.1 and its October 1, 2026 effective date in credit memos, since thresholds changed between versions.
- **Match the DSCR to the scenario.** Apply 1.10, 1.15, or 1.25 based on loan size and type rather than one blanket ratio.
- **Call former franchisees.** Item 20 lists franchisees who left the system in the last fiscal year, which gives underwriters direct access to operator experience.
- **Request Item 19 substantiation.** The FTC Rule requires franchisors to provide written substantiation for performance claims on reasonable request.
- **Evaluate franchisor support directly.** Use Item 21 financials and franchisee reference calls to judge whether the franchisor can sustain training, marketing, and operational support.


#### Common Pitfalls to Avoid


- **Treating Directory listing as a credit signal.** SBA explicitly states that listing does not endorse or guarantee a brand's success.
- **Reading Item 20 closures as a defined failure rate.** Calling a closure a failure is an analytic choice, so define your method and apply it consistently.
- **Using vendor scores as causal proof.** Brand scores can inform segmentation, but published vendor results describe historical charge-offs rather than guaranteed future performance.
- **Assuming all franchisors are audited.** Start-up franchisors may provide unaudited statements during the FTC phase-in period.


### Key Takeaways for Franchise Lenders


Franchise financing underwriting works best when unit-level and brand-level risk are scored separately, then combined into one decision. The unit must clear cash flow, equity, guaranty, and collateral tests, and the brand must hold up under FDD Items 7, 19, 20, and 21.


SOP 50 10 8.1 raised coverage for initial acquisitions to 1.25:1 and requires Directory listing for SBA franchise loans. Lenders outside the SBA program can use these thresholds as a reference standard, then calibrate them to their own portfolio data and credit appetite.

### Frequently Asked Questions About Franchise Financing Underwriting


#### What Documents Do Lenders Require for a Franchise Loan?


Lenders typically require the FDD, the franchise agreement, borrower and franchisor cash flow projections, equity source records, guarantor information, and a collateral schedule. Acquisitions also require the seller's historical financials covering the last fiscal year-end or two years.


#### What Is the Minimum DSCR for an SBA Franchise Loan?


Under SOP 50 10 8.1, standard 7(a) loans require 1.15:1 and 7(a) Small loans of $350,000 or less require 1.10:1. Initial acquisitions and owner buyouts require 1.25:1.


#### How Much Equity Does a Franchisee Need to Inject?


SBA requires at least 10% of total project costs for start-ups operating one year or less and for change-of-ownership loans. The requirement cannot be reduced for initial acquisitions, though some business expansions and owner buyouts may qualify for a reduction.


#### Does SBA Franchise Directory Listing Mean a Brand Is Low Risk?


No, because SBA states that placement on the Directory is not an endorsement or guaranty of a brand's success. Listing confirms eligibility, so lenders still need to assess brand quality through the FDD and franchisor data.


#### Do SBA Rules Apply to Conventional Franchise Loans?


SBA 7(a) and 504 rules do not bind conventional or fintech loans. Credit teams can use SBA thresholds as a reference point when setting their own franchise lending policy.
